newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian hardliners blast Moscow-NATO deal.
newsitem.headline: Russian hardliners blast Moscow-NATO deal.

text.p: Russian hardliners predictably attacked Wednesday's deal on future relations with NATO, while liberal politicians and experts took a cautious line, waiting for more details to emerge.

"(The West) has often cheated Russia and they will probably cheat us this time as well because we have nothing to trade with," Albert Makashov, a communist deputy in the State Duma lower house of parliament, told reporters.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said on Wednesday that after tough talks they had finally come to terms on the document aimed at mapping out relations beween Moscow and the Western alliance.

Solana told a joint news conference the deal, also intended to address some of Moscow's concerns about NATO expansion, could be ready for signing in Paris on May 27 after President Boris Yeltsin and leaders of the 16 alliance members approve it.
Primakov and Solana gave no details about the document but stressed that both sides were tough in negotiating to win as many concessions as possible.

A Russian Communist Party leader, Anatoly Lukyanov, said he was impressed by Primakov's tough bargaining but suggested the deal, hammered out by the minister with little space for manouevre, was unlikely to win wide public backing.

"Our contacts with Primakov in the Duma and in the Foreign Ministry show that he defended the only possible option," Lukyanov told reporters. "But in our opinion the agreement itself cannot be welcomed by society and cannot prompt positive emotions among deputies."
Lukyanov said that, whatever the compromise, bargaining over the deal was humiliating for Russia.
"There is a battle raging over NATO expansion," he said. "But this is not a battle of equals."
In the course of talks, which started in January, Moscow said repeatedly it disapproved of NATO's decision to invite several eastern European countries to join the alliance.
But Russian leaders have said that a say in NATO decision-making and a firm promise never to move the alliance's military infrastructure eastwards could dispel some of its security concerns.
NATO said it had no plans to move forces to the east but has refused to give any formal guarantees for the future, arguing that this would hamper the rights of new members.
Centrist deputy Duma speaker Alexander Shokhin said that without meeting these demands NATO could hardly count on widespread support in Russia.

But he told Reuters: "If NATO, through Solana, agreed not to put nuclear weapons on the territory of new members and not to build new military bases, then indeed it (the agreement) was a breakthrough."
Grigory Yavlinsky, a leader of a strong liberal Yabloko party, also sought details of the deal, which may not be made public until it is approved by the leaders of Russia and 16 NATO countries.
But he added that many crucial things were still to be defined in the course of future talks.
"My main wish is that Russia continue deep and important discussions with NATO because this is important to Russian foreign policy in decades to come," he told Reuters.
